column2: Beyond this is the more secret matter, the supreme self-knowledge above the human, which was seen by the great sages and is sung in the Vedanta; that I shall tell you, which you ask me."
[Vyasa said:] "That which is the self-knowledge of man here, dear, I shall tell you; hear this explanation of it.
Earth, water, light, wind and space are the great elements of beings, like the waves of the sea.
As a tortoise draws back its limbs after extending them, so the great elements are modified in the lesser.
Thus all this, moving and unmoving, is made of that; and so it is taught at creation and at dissolution.
The maker of beings made the five great elements in all beings, dear, and in them he sees difference."
[Shuka said:] "What he made in bodies, how may it be known? And the senses and the qualities, how may they be known?"
[Vyasa said:] "I shall tell you this view here as it is; hear the truth here one-pointed, how it is.
Sound, hearing and the cavities: these three are born of space; breath, movement and touch: these are the three qualities of wind.
Form, the eye and digestion are ordained as the threefold fire; taste, tongue and moisture are these three qualities of water.
The smellable, the nose and the body are the three qualities of earth. So much has been explained of the group of senses made of the five elements.
Touch belongs to wind, taste to water, form is said to belong to light; sound arises from space, and smell is held to be the quality of earth.
Mind, intellect and feeling: these three are born of the self; they do not pass beyond the qualities and are held to be beyond the qualities.
In a man there are five senses, and the mind is said to rest in them; they call intellect the seventh and the knower of the field again the eighth.
The eye is for seeing; the mind makes doubt; intellect is for determination; the knower of the field is called the witness.
Rajas, tamas and sattva: these three, born of their own womb, are equal in all beings; one should know them in their qualities.
As a tortoise extends its limbs here and withdraws them, so intellect, having created the host of senses, restrains it.
That which sees upward from the soles of the feet and downward from the head: in this very work the supreme intellect acts.
Intellect leads the qualities; intellect also leads the senses, all with the mind as resting-place; without intellect, where are the qualities?
There, whatever is joined with joy one finds in the self, as if calm and perfectly pure, take as sattva.
What is joined with torment in body or mind should be rajas, the mover, always carrying off embodied beings.
And what is joined with delusion, whose object is unmanifest, beyond reasoning and unknowable, take that as tamas.
Joy, delight, bliss, equanimity, steadiness of mind, whether from cause or none: the sattvic quality.
Conceit, falsehood, greed, delusion and impatience are the marks of rajas, which occur with and without cause.
Likewise delusion, heedlessness, drowsiness, sleep and wakefulness, occurring somehow, are to be known as tamasic qualities."
[Vyasa said:] "Beyond the senses are the objects; beyond the objects, the mind; beyond the mind, intellect; beyond intellect, the self is held supreme.
Intellect is the self of man; intellect is the self of his self; when it changes state, it becomes mind.
By the separateness of the senses, intellect changes: hearing, it becomes the ear; touching, it is called touch.
Seeing, it becomes sight; tasting, the tongue; smelling, the nose; intellect changes separately.
They are called senses; the unseen one rules in them; intellect, abiding in the Person, acts in three states.
Sometimes it finds delight, sometimes it grieves; it is never joined here with pleasure or pain.
This, of the nature of states, does not pass beyond these three states, like the lord of rivers, the ocean, with its waves, its great shore.
When it desires something, it becomes mind. One should recall these supports separately by intellect; the senses alone are to be conquered wholly, and are pure.
A man should make a lamp-purpose by the senses, best of understanding, going forth as appropriate, indifferent, at will.
Thus this is by nature, so the learned is not bewildered, not grieving, not exulting, ever free of envy.
For the self cannot be seen by senses that range at will, driven wrongly and hard to hold by the unself-controlled.
When he rightly restrains their rays by the mind, then the self shines, like a lamp burning in a pot, as when darkness has gone for all beings.
As a water-bird moving in water is not stained by it, so the one of trained wisdom, moving among objects, is not stained by faults; unattached to all, he is in no way stained.
Giving up deeds done before, ever delighting in the self, the self of all beings, unattached to the paths of the qualities,
the self sometimes brings forth sattva or the qualities; the qualities do not know the self, but he always knows the qualities.
He is the watcher of the qualities and truly their creator; know this difference between sattva and the knower of the field, both subtle.
One creates the qualities and the other does not; by nature they are distinct, and always joined.
As fish and water, though distinct, are joined, so are those two; and as gnat and fig-tree are joined together,
or as the reed in the munja grass is both apart and together, so these two are together, established in each other."
[Vyasa said:] "All that creates these qualities is joined with its own nature, as a spider creates its thread; the qualities are like threads.
Those destroyed do not return; activity is not found; some decide thus, others that there is withdrawal.
Having weighed both, one should decide according to judgment; by this rule one becomes a great one lying in the womb.
Having reached the beginningless, endless, eternal, a man should move about, not angry, not exultant, ever free of envy.
Thus, having crossed the firm knot of the heart made of thoughts of intellect, one should sit happy, not grieving, his doubts cut.
As men fallen from the ground would suffer in a full river, plunging in, so know this world of the unlearned.
But the learned one does not suffer; the knower of truth walks on dry ground; so he who finds the self finds the sole knowledge of the self.
Knowing thus, a man, considering slowly and rightly the coming and going of all beings, gains the highest peace.
Knowing this, one becomes awakened; what other mark of the awakened is there? Knowing this, the wise are freed, their work done.
For the learned there is no great fear of what is a very great fear for the unlearned; there is no higher goal for anyone than the eternal one of the learned.
People envy the world of the afflicted and grieve looking at this and that; there see the skilled who do not grieve, who know both, done and undone.
What one does without prior intent, and what he did before, that he drives away; neither is dear or undear to him as he acts here."
[Vyasa said:] "I shall tell you the ancient dharma praised by the sages, excellent above all dharmas; hear it here one-pointed.
Having carefully restrained by intellect the senses, which are destructive, springing out on every side, as a father his young sons,
the one-pointedness of the mind and senses is the highest austerity; that is better than all dharmas; that dharma is called supreme.
Having joined them all, resting in the mind, by understanding, he should sit as if satisfied in the self, thinking nothing of what is much to be thought.
When they are turned back from the fields of sense and stay in their house, then you will see the Supreme, the eternal, by the self in the self.
The great-souled brahmanas who are wise see him, the self of all, the great soul, like smokeless fire.
As a great tree with many branches, endowed with flowers and fruit, does not know of itself, "where is my flower, where my fruit?"
so the self does not know, "where shall I go, whence am I?"; there is another within who sees all, the inner self.
Freed from all sins, as a snake from its sloughed skin, having gained the highest understanding here, free of sin and fever,
cross the dreadful river with currents on every side, that carries the world's flow, with the five senses as crocodiles and the intentions of the mind as banks,
covered with the grass of greed and delusion, with desire and anger as reptiles, truth as its ford, falsehood as its turbulence, anger its mud, the best of rivers,
whose source is the unmanifest, swift, hard for the unself-controlled to cross; cross the river by intellect, crowded with the crocodiles of desire,
going to the ocean of the world, hard to cross for the pit of wombs, born of the self's own birth, dear, with whirlpools of the tongue, hard to approach.
The steadfast wise of trained wisdom cross it; having crossed it, freed on every side, purified in self, a knower of the self, pure,
resorting to the highest understanding, you will go to the state of Brahman, having crossed all afflictions, serene of soul, free of stain.
Look on beings as one standing on a mountain on those on the ground, not angry, not exultant, with a merciful mind; then you will see the origin and dissolution of all beings.
Thus the wise held this dharma as excellent above all dharmas, best of those who uphold dharma, the sages who see the truth.
Knowing the self to be imperishable, this teaching to a son should be told to one who is restrained, for his good, and following.
This secret self-knowledge, the most secret of all secrets, great, I have told you directly, dear, witnessed by the self.
This is neither woman nor man nor neuter; it is without pain and without pleasure, Brahman, of the nature of past, future and becoming.
Knowing this, neither man nor woman reaches rebirth again; this path is ordained for the attainment of non-existence.
Then all the views are not, as I have told them, son, in just this way; they are and are not.
To a son endowed with love and virtue, with the qualities of a good son, asked with affection for his good, a father should say here what has been said."
[Vyasa said:] "One who studies all the Vedas, serving with celibacy, the Riks, Yajuses and Samans, is not by that a brahmana.
One who is kin to all beings, knowing all, knowing all Vedas, who never dies without desire, is not by that a brahmana.
Having performed varied sacrifices and rites with the proper fees, he never gains brahminhood through mere meditation.
When he does not fear and others do not fear him, when he neither desires nor hates, then he attains Brahman.
When he does no evil toward any being in deed, mind or speech, then he attains Brahman.
Desire is the one bond; there is no other bond here; freed from the bond of desire, one becomes fit for Brahman.
Freed from desire, like the moon from smoky cloud, free of dust, wishing for desire, the steadfast acts with steadiness.
As waters enter the ocean that is being filled and is unmoving in its place, so he whom desires enter but who does not desire desires, the embodied one, goes from the world to heaven.
The secret of austerity is renunciation; of renunciation, happiness; of happiness, heaven; of heaven, peace.
Wetness, grief of mind, torment with craving: you wish for sattva; from contentment comes the highest mark, peace.
Free of grief, free of mine-ness, calm, serene of soul, the best knower of the self, he who has these marks, complete, will come again.
By wise men endowed with sattva and with counsellors beyond measure, those who know the self after death are known as such here.
Not artificial, not to be taken, natural, unadorned, self-knowledge: one of good deeds and wisdom enjoys imperishable happiness.
Having made the mind free of wandering and established it on every side, the contentment he gains cannot be otherwise.
He by whom one is satisfied without eating, content without wealth, bears strength without oil: whoever knows him is a knower of the Veda.
The brahmana who stays, guarding the doors of the self, closing them and reflecting, is called delighting in the self, refined.
Collected in the Supreme, desire spent, standing, happiness follows him on every side like the moon's body.
For the sage who resorts to beings with distinctions and to qualities, pain is easily driven off, as darkness by the sun.
Old age and death do not find the brahmana who has gone beyond action, beyond the spending of qualities, even if clinging to objects.
When he stands freed on every side, equal, he passes beyond the senses and sense objects while in the body.
Having reached the highest cause, having passed beyond the state of effect, for him who has reached the supreme beyond the supreme there is no return."
[Vyasa said:] "Space, wind, light, water and earth as fifth, being and non-being and time: in all beings these five.
Space is the inner self; hearing, the sense, is made of it; know its quality as sound, knower of the form and the rule of the shastras.
Movement is of the nature of wind; prana and apana are made of it; know the touch sense, and touch too, as made of it.
Then cooking and light, fire and the eye are made of it; know its quality as form, with darkness as its unfinished nature.
Wetness, smallness, oiliness: this is taught of water; the tongue is the sense, and taste is held the quality of water.
The earthy constituent is the compound: bone, teeth and nails, beard, hair and head hair, veins, sinew and skin.
The sense named smell is called the nose; and smell is to be known as made of earth, this sense and its object.
In the later ones are all the qualities, and in all the later; the sages know the continuity of the groups of the five elements.
Mind is the ninth of these, intellect the tenth, and the inner self the eleventh, said to be beyond all.
Intellect is of the nature of resolve, mind of the nature of expression; from inference by action it is known; that is the soul, called the field.
The wise one who sees the stainless that pervades all with all these states, whose last is time, does not follow delusion."
[Vyasa said:] "As rays move together, going, standing and being seen, so beings beyond the human, freed from bodies, roam the worlds.
As the sun's heat is seen reflected in water, so one endowed with sattva sees the reflection of sattva.
Those subtle ones, freed from the body, are seen by the knowers of truth, abiding in goodness and restrained in senses, by their own truth.
What is thought by the self of all, sleeping and waking, joined with a division of the primal, giving up the dust born of action.
As by day so by night, as by night so by day, the sattvic self stays in control for yogis of yoga.
For them the ever-eternal self of beings is always joined with seven qualities, subtle, moving, ageless and deathless.
Overcome by mind and intellect, knowing his own and another's body, in dreams too he becomes the knower of pleasure and pain.
There too he gets pain, there too pleasure; there too, having done anger and greed, he meets calamity.
Becoming devoted to the discipline of scripture, wishing to find their own self, those formless ones without breath, though like thunderbolts,
in the four stages and their actions created separately, Shandilya called this yoga in concentration peace.
Knowing the seven subtle ones and the six-limbed great Lord, standing in the application of the primal, he reaches the supreme Brahman."
[Vyasa said:] "Its basis is ignorance; heedlessness is the sprinkling; envy is the leaf; and it is full of the essence of former evil.
Its grief-branches are delusion, worry and torment, and it is terrible, wound round by creepers of bewildering thirst.
The very greedy, wishing for fruit, serve this great tree; bound by toils and snares, they surround its fruits.
He who, having brought those snares under control, uproots that tree, has gone to the end of both sorrows, striving for both.
The one of untrained wisdom climbs the tree in torment, and it kills him, like a poison, like a draught to a sick man.
The root of its remaining, for it is pulled up by force, by the sword of equanimity made by renunciation and heedfulness.
He who thus knows the mere dragging of desire, the killing of the science of desire, passes beyond sorrows.
They call the body a city and intellect is held the mistress; there the mind, named the thinker of aims, stays in the body.
When the mind becomes separate from intellect and alone, then it lies there, open, empty, and rajas remains.
That mind makes friendship, joined with rajas, and, taking the townsfolk, gives them to rajas."
[Vyasa said:] "The blessed one, like a blazing fire, spoke to Dhumravarchas; then I too shall give a further example, son.
The earth's steadiness, breadth, hardness, power of generation, smell, heaviness, strength, compactness, support and firmness.
Of the waters, coldness, taste, wetness, fluidity, oiliness, gentleness, tongue that flows, and earthy-watery oozing.
Of fire, unassailability, energy, heat, cooking, lighting, purity, passion, lightness, sharpness, and as tenth, rising upward.
Of wind, lack of restraint, touch, place of speech, independence, strength, speed, delusion and the effort made by action.
Of space, the quality sound, pervasiveness, holes, being without support, without resting-place, unmanifest, and unchangingness.
Unobstructedness, elementhood and modifications: fifty qualities are spoken, nourished by the nature of the five elements.
Mobility, expression, release, imagining, forbearance, being and non-being and quickness: these are the nine qualities of the mind."

[Bhishma said:] "They say there are sixty qualities of beings, attached to eminence in beings, ever clinging, attached to beings and made by the imperishable; but, son, they do not say they are eternal.
What has been said is measured by thought, son; the future is yours here; having reached all that, the truth of the meaning of beings, be of calm mind by the power of beings."
[Yudhishthira said:] "Each of terrible strength, and of the strength of ten thousand elephants; these have been slain in battle by men of equal energy and strength.
I do not see who was the slayer of these in battle before; they were endowed with valour, with energy and strength.
Now these, greatly wise one, lie lifeless, and this word "dead" is used of these lifeless ones.
These kings, mostly of terrible valour, are dead; there arises doubt in me: whence the word "dead"?
Whose is death, whence is death, and by whom does death here carry off creatures, like the immortals? Tell me that, grandsire."
[Bhishma said:] "Long ago, dear, in the Krita age, there was a king named Avikampana; he fell under the power of his enemy in battle, his vehicles spent.
There his son, named Hari, equal to Narayana in strength, was slain in battle by enemies, with his army and followers.
That king, under his enemies' power and filled with grief for his son, by chance, intent on peace, saw Narada on the earth."
Hearing his words, the ascetic Narada then told this tale, which removes grief for a son.

King, hear this very long tale, as it happened, and as I too have heard it, lord of the earth.
mahabharata:12:248.13	At the creation of beings, the Grandfather of great energy, having created beings, could not bear the beings that had grown very numerous.
mahabharata:12:248.14	There was no gap anywhere for creatures, Achyuta; the three worlds, king, were as if bound, without breath.
mahabharata:12:248.15	A thought arose in him about destruction, lord of the earth; thinking, he found no reason or cause for dissolution.
mahabharata:12:248.16	From his anger, great king, fire rose from the cavities; with it the Grandfather burnt all the directions, king.
mahabharata:12:248.17	Then fire, born of the blessed one's wrath, burnt heaven, earth and sky, and the world with its moving and unmoving, king.
mahabharata:12:248.18	There beings, moving and fixed, were burnt by the great force of the anger of the great-grandfather in his wrath.
mahabharata:12:248.19	Then Sthanu, Hari, Shiva, lord of the Vedic sacrifice, the slayer of heroes, went for refuge to Brahma.
mahabharata:12:248.20	When Sthanu had come, for the good of the subjects, the boon-giving god, blazing as it were, said to Shiva:
mahabharata:12:248.21	'What wish shall I fulfil today? You are held by me worthy of a boon; I shall do what pleases you, Shambhu, whatever is in your heart.'
[Sthanu said:] "By the fire of your energy, god, the subjects are burnt everywhere; seeing them, I feel pity; do not be angry with them, lord of the world."
[Prajapati said:] "I am not angry, nor do I desire that the beings not be; for the lightening of the earth, destruction is wished.
This goddess, distressed by her burden, has always urged me for destruction, great god; by the burden she sinks in the waters.
Since I found by intellect, thinking much, no way to destroy these grown ones, anger entered me."
[Sthanu said:] "Be gracious at the end of destruction, lord of the thirty gods; do not be angry; do not destroy the beings, moving and unmoving.
All pools, all grass and shrubs, the unmoving and moving, the fourfold host of beings:
all this world has been reduced to ashes and overwhelmed; be gracious, blessed good one; this boon is chosen by me.
Destroyed, these subjects will never come back; therefore turn this energy back by your own energy."
[Narada said:] Hearing Sthanu's words, the god, with restrained speech and mind, drew his own energy back into himself.
Then, taking back the fire, the blessed one honoured by the worlds ordained both activity and withdrawal, the lord.
As he withdrew that fire born of anger, there appeared from all the cavities a woman of the great soul.
Dark, in red garments, with red eyes and palms, with divine earrings and shining with divine ornaments.
Coming out of the cavities, she took to the southern direction; the two, the girl and the god, lords of the universe, saw each other.
Calling her, the god, the primal lord of the worlds, said, "Death! Slay these subjects, lord of the earth.
For you were thought of by me in my anger with the purpose of destruction; therefore destroy all these subjects, wise one.
Destroy the subjects without distinction, lady; by my command you will attain the highest good."
Thus addressed, the goddess Death, wearing a lotus garland, a young girl, pondered grieved, with a great fall of tears.
The lord of men caught those tears in his hands, and again begged for the good of mankind."
[Death said:] "How could a woman like me be born of you, best of speakers, to be of dreadful deeds, terrifying to all creatures?
I fear adharma; assign me a righteous task; look on me, fearful, with an auspicious eye, lord.
I would not take away children, the aged and those in youth who are blameless; creatures, lord of creatures, I bow to you; be gracious to me.
I fear for the dear sons, friends, brothers, mothers and fathers who, god, will think ill of me when they are dead.
The wetness of the tears of the wretched would burn me for ever; mightily afraid of them, I have come to you for refuge.
In Yama's house, god, the sinful go in the end; I appease you, giver of boons; grant me favour, lord.
This is the wish I desire from you, Grandfather of the world; I wish by your grace to practise austerity, lord of the gods."
[The Grandfather said:] "Death, you were imagined by me for the purpose of destroying the subjects; go, destroy all subjects, and do not hesitate."
Though told again and again, she, the lady, as if lifeless, remained silent; then the god, lord of the lords of gods,
was pleased, Brahma himself with his own self, self-possessed; and smiling, the lord of the world looked at all the worlds.
When the anger of the blessed unconquered one had ceased, the girl, we have heard, went away from his presence.
Going aside, not promising the destruction of the subjects, Death then, as if in haste, went to Dhenuka, king.
There the goddess performed the supreme, hard austerity; for years she stood on one foot, ten times a thousand million and five.
As she performed there that supremely hard austerity, again Brahma of great splendour spoke:
Do my word, Death. Disregarding it hastily, she stood in the same way on one foot, and then seven others.
She stood for five and two lotuses more, giver of honour, and then a hundred thousand million she roamed with the deer.
Going again then, king, she took up the highest silence in the waters for seven thousand years, king.
Then the girl went to the Kaushiki, bull of the Bharatas; there, living on wind and water, she performed her rule again.
Then the greatly fortunate one went to the Ganga and to Meru alone; she stood motionless like a log, wishing the good of beings.
Then, on the head of the Himalaya, where the gods had sacrificed, king of kings, she stood on her thumb a hundred thousand years more, and with effort pleased the Grandfather.
Then the origin and dissolution of the worlds said to her there: "What is this, daughter? Do my word."
The king, saying "he is poor and not of my class," was not willing to give his daughter Sudarshana to that brahmana.
His son was Marutta, mighty, equal to Vasava; the earth, girdled by the sea, was devoted to him.
I think what was to be has come to you, lord of men; by good fortune, serving you, I shall be freed from the fever of my mind.
Blessed one, you have mostly destroyed everything, Achyuta; seek Rama's footprint; let us go where he is.
Hearing the king's words, Indra, king of the gods, Purandara, answered Yudhishthira with words joined with non-cruelty.
See your brothers and the other kings of your side, each arrived at his own place; let the fever of your mind go.
